read_scope.notes: Independently verified sha256 of manuscript/paper.pdf (136e1777...) and RUBRIC.md (e3c0d440...) against input_hashes.json; both match. Read RUBRIC.md in full first. Read the complete layout-preserving manuscript.txt (all 1,249 lines, pages 1-22 including Appendices A-G), then visually inspected all 22 rendered pages as images (pages/page-01.png through page-22.png), including main Figures 1-3 (pp. 4, 7, 8), appendix Figures 4-5 (p. 20) and Tables 1-12 (pp. 3, 7, 8, 9, 10, 16, 17, 19, 21). Additionally zoomed crops of Figure 1 (p. 4, GPT Image 2 row) and Figure 2 (p. 7, GPT Image 1/2 panels) to check legibility of the small multiples and the M/S/P detail insets. Consulted manuscript/paper.tex and the included specificity_*.tex fragments only to resolve notation and table/figure sources; counted the abstract at 154 words (limit 155) and checked arithmetic consistency of Tables 2, 4 and 8. No repository, network, other reviewer material or other manuscript versions accessed; no files edited.

score_reasons.expression: Sentences are short and controlled (mean ~18 words in the main text), terminology is stable across 10 pages of main text and 12 pages of appendices (contrast, aligned response β, error D, shared vs between-name, declared vs retrospective), and transitions carry the argument (§5.1 'Yet positive alignment does not ensure low error'; §5.4 italic run-in heads 'Averaging scenes.' / 'Rescaling contrasts.'). Material weaknesses remain. First, qualification is not economical: roughly 29 explicit negative-disclaimer constructions appear in ~4,250 main-text words, and nearly every paragraph and caption closes with one (§4.3 'They neither isolate... nor establish...'; §5.4 'Neither interpretation determines whether such variation is artistically appropriate'; Tables 1, 3, 4, 11 and Figures 3, 4, 5 captions each end with a similar clause). The repetition flattens emphasis so the two or three limits that actually bound the conclusions do not stand out. Second, a referent is genuinely ambiguous: §5.4's 'The fitted multipliers scale every contrast coordinate by about 0.45' reads as a statement about all six models, but Appendix C.2 gives .438-.459 for GPT Image 2 and .598-.694 for FLUX. Third, 'brief' is used as a synonym for the fixed scene text from the Figure 1 caption onward without ever being defined. Minor: numeric style alternates between prose (.999 [.893, 1.104]) and tables (0.999 [0.893, 1.104]); the Introduction's closing 'This controlled empirical audit uses established estimators' is self-characterizing and carries no information.
score_reasons.structure: The progression is coherent and signposted: question and why conflation matters (§1), positioning (§2), panels/design/features (§3), what agreement means then how it is computed then how it is tested (§4.1-4.4), results in a deliberate order (aligned response vs error, shared component, pair diagnostics, scene averaging and calibration, reference sensitivity), then discussion, scope and conclusion. Hierarchy of evidence is visible and repeatedly re-stated: the 21-endpoint prespecified family versus explicitly retrospective diagnostics (§4.4, §5.3-5.5, Appendix C's title 'Post-result target diagnostics'), with Table 4 and Table 5 captions marking bold minima and reused intervals as non-confirmatory. The main-text/appendix split is defensible: Appendices A-G hold feature definitions, estimator identities, controls, coverage simulations, provenance and earlier cohorts, and the main text remains readable without them. Concrete weaknesses: §4.4 largely previews and partly restates §4.3, adding a section boundary for little content; §5.5's heading promises a survivorship summary but the corrected error estimates are reported only for FLUX (.801 → .872), so the section's own claim cannot be checked from the page; Table 2 makes FLUX the ΔD baseline while Eq. 7 in Appendix B.2 fixes γ at GPT Image 2, an unexplained switch of reference model; and §5.1's key negative statement ('the other 13 intervals include zero') depends on Table 10, which sits in Appendix E on p. 19.
score_reasons.new_reader_understanding: This is the manuscript's strongest dimension. The abstract stands alone at 154 words and states design, headline share, the negative benchmark result and the perceptual-fidelity limit. Motivation is concrete (§1: moving closer to Monet does not show that Monet and Sisley differences are reproduced). The arms are unambiguous (six clauses, 14 scenes, two repeats, 1,008 images = 6×14×6×2) and the reference target is defined as a finite digital reproduction panel, explicitly 'not a perceptually validated definition of style'. Intuition precedes notation throughout: §4.1 gives a single-feature worked example (Monet .325 development-IQR units below Sisley; GPT Image 2 .254 in the same direction) and three idealized generators anchoring expected D at 1, 0 and 1 before any symbol appears in §4.2. Every metric carries its anchors in the caption (β = 1 matches reference strength; D = 0 exact, 1 no distinction; Q = 1 reference size), units are explained as development-panel IQRs rather than perceptual units, and Table 1 translates the 31 features into plain properties. Limits are collected in §6.1 and the repository is not needed to follow the argument. Remaining gaps: the corrected-source error values for the other five models are never shown (§5.5, C.5), so 'Source correction preserves FLUX's lowest point estimate' is unverifiable within the paper; 'repeat-corrected squared change' appears in the abstract and Table 3 before repeat correction is explained in §4.2, and the within-scene variant (88.6-97.2%, Appendix B) never surfaces in the main text, leaving a reader unsure which number is the headline; 'brief' is undefined; and Figure 2's overview panels compress all four painter means into the left third of each axis, so the actual comparison is legible only in the small insets.
score_reasons.engagement: The question is consequential and clearly framed as a discrimination problem rather than a leaderboard: does a painter's name reproduce painter differences, or mostly repaint? The narrative has genuine turns that are explained through what they reveal — GPT Image 2 matches the reference-aligned amplitude almost exactly (β = .999) yet has D = 1.226; FLUX has the lowest error with a much weaker response (β = .470); the aggregate hides near-zero or reversed Monet-Sisley alignment in five models (Figure 3a, -0.25 to 0.13); and scalar calibration flips the ordering to GPT Image 2 (.554 vs .714, Table 4). Figure 1 rewards inspection: a 7×6 grid with both control arms, a caption that tells the reader what to compare, and a checkable single-cell claim (GPT Image 2's Cezanne trees are visibly darker blue-green than its Monet and Sisley trees, confirmed on zoom). Figure 3's paired heatmaps are scannable and carry the paper's most interesting reversal. Tone is disciplined with no hype. What holds it back: Figure 2, the main results figure, does not reward inspection — roughly half of each overview panel is empty space and the faint scene/repeat dots are barely visible; §5.5 and the closing appendices settle into dense number recitation; and the constant terminal disclaimers suppress emphasis exactly where a finding has just landed, so several paragraphs end on a retraction rather than on the point.

strengths: Intuition before notation is executed well: §4.1 introduces contrasts with a single-feature Monet-Sisley lightness example and three idealized generators (expected D = 1, 0, 1) so that §4.2's estimators arrive already interpreted.
Metric anchors are restated wherever numbers appear: Table 2, Table 4, Table 8 and Figure 3 captions all define β = 1, D = 0/1 and Q = 1, so no figure or table requires a return trip to §4.

The prespecified/retrospective boundary is consistently visible (§4.3's 21-endpoint family, §4.4, Appendix C's title, Table 5's 'reuse that procedure retrospectively and add no confirmatory tests', Table 4's 'Bold marks each error column's minimum, not significance'), so a reader never has to guess which results carry inferential weight.

Figure 1 (p. 4) is a genuinely inspectable 7×6 grid that includes both the artist-free and generic-painting controls and a caption instructing the reader how to read it; the in-text claim about GPT Image 2's Cezanne trees is verifiable by eye.

Figure 3 (p. 8) surfaces the paper's most interesting result — uneven, sometimes reversed painter-pair alignment — in one scannable pair of heatmaps with a diverging scale centered on the meaningful values.
Reported quantities are internally consistent and checkable: D = D_aggregate + V_scene holds across Table 4, and D = 1 - 2β + Q reproduces Table 2's D from Table 8's Q for every model.
The abstract is standalone and 154 words, inside the 155-word limit, and ends on the correct scope limit rather than a claim of perceptual fidelity.

findings.issue: The source-correction analysis reports corrected error estimates only for FLUX (.801 → .832 with original scaling, .872 after refitting) and three pairwise differences against FLUX. The section's own conclusion, 'Source correction preserves FLUX's lowest point estimate', and the related claim that 'GPT Image 2 retains the lowest calibrated estimate (.579)' cannot be checked, because the corrected D and D_held values for the other five models appear nowhere in the paper.
findings.reader_effect: A reader is asked to accept the robustness conclusion on assertion at exactly the point where the manuscript says source handling 'has a more consequential effect on statistical comparisons'. The section heading promises a survivorship summary that the evidence on the page does not support.
findings.suggested_change: Add one line of six numbers to Appendix C.5 (no new analysis, no length cost), e.g. 'Corrected uncalibrated D after refitting: GPT Image 1 x.xxx, GPT Image 2 x.xxx, Flare x.xxx, Sunburst x.xxx, Nano Banana 2 x.xxx, FLUX .872 (calibrated D_held: ..., FLUX ..., GPT Image 2 .579).' Then §5.5 can keep its one-sentence summary and cite C.5.

findings.location: §5.4, 'Rescaling contrasts' paragraph (p. 9), sentence beginning 'The fitted multipliers scale every contrast coordinate by about 0.45'
findings.issue: The sentence has no stated subject and follows a GPT Image 2 discussion, so it reads as a property of all six models' calibration. Appendix C.2 shows the multipliers differ substantially by model: GPT Image 2 .438-.459, FLUX .598-.694.
findings.reader_effect: A reader carries forward a wrong mental model of the calibration — a single ~0.45 shrinkage applied across the panel — and so misreads why calibration reorders the models (it shrinks the high-magnitude models far more than FLUX).
findings.suggested_change: Replace with: 'GPT Image 2's fitted multipliers are about 0.45 and FLUX's about 0.65, each fitted only on the other 13 scenes (Appendix C.2).'

findings.issue: The overview axes run to about +4 on axis 1 and +4/-2 on axis 2, while every plotted mean sits between roughly -2 and +2 on axis 1 and -1 and +1 on axis 2 except Cezanne. Roughly half of each panel is empty, the four painter means and their matching-label lines overlap at the left, and the faint scene/repeat dots are barely resolvable at print size; the comparison the caption asks for happens only inside the small M/S/P insets.
findings.reader_effect: The paper's main results figure does not reward inspection: at a glance a reader sees one separated pink point per model and an undifferentiated cluster, and must rely on the inset to see the Monet/Sisley/Pissarro behaviour that §5.1 and §5.3 depend on.
findings.suggested_change: Tighten the overview x- and y-limits to the plotted range (about -2.5 to 2.5 on axis 1), or drop the overview entirely and enlarge each model to a single panel at the detail scale with Cezanne shown as a small corner inset. Same six panels, same data, no page cost.

findings.location: §3.2 (p. 2) onward; first use in the Figure 1 caption (p. 4, 'one brief'); then §4.3, §5.4, §5.5, Table 7 (p. 16), Figures 4-5 captions (p. 20)
findings.issue: 'Brief' is used interchangeably with 'scene' roughly a dozen times but is never defined. §3.2 introduces 'Fourteen authored outdoor scenes'; the reader first meets 'brief' in a figure caption and must infer that a brief is the fixed scene text.
findings.reader_effect: A reader without project knowledge briefly wonders whether 'briefs' are a second design factor alongside scenes (particularly in Table 7's '11 common briefs / 14 briefs' column heads and §6.1's '14 authored briefs'), which costs re-reading at each occurrence.
findings.suggested_change: In §3.2, after 'Fourteen authored outdoor scenes span water, built, land and mixed compositions', add four words: 'we call each fixed scene text a brief'. Then use one term consistently in headings and column heads.

findings.location: Abstract (p. 1), §5.2 heading and text (p. 8), Table 3 (p. 8), Appendix B (p. 14)
findings.issue: The headline share (82.5-95.7%) is the scene-averaged, repeat-corrected variant, while Appendix B reports a within-scene variant with a different range (88.6-97.2%) that never appears in the main text. The main text does not say why the scene-averaged variant is the headline, and §5.2's heading ('Most measured change is common to the painter names') drops the qualification that the body sentence carries.
findings.reader_effect: A reader who reaches Appendix B finds a second, higher set of numbers for what looks like the same quantity and cannot tell which is primary or why they differ, weakening confidence in the paper's single most quoted statistic.
findings.suggested_change: In §5.2, after the Table 3 sentence, add one clause: 'Computing the split within each scene before averaging gives higher shares (88.6-97.2%, Appendix B); we report the scene-averaged version because it matches the scene-averaged target used for D.'

findings.location: Main text and captions throughout, e.g. §4.3 (p. 6), §5.3 last sentence (p. 8), §5.4 last sentence (p. 9), Table 1, Table 3, Table 11, Figure 4 and Figure 5 captions
findings.issue: Approximately 29 terminal disclaimer constructions ('does not establish', 'do not', 'cannot', 'need not') appear in about 4,250 main-text words, several of which restate the same two limits (measurements are not perceptual style; descriptive results are not tests).
findings.reader_effect: Momentum drops at the end of almost every paragraph, and because all caveats are stated with equal weight, the genuinely binding ones (the digital-reproduction target; no model beats D = 1) do not stand out from routine ones.
findings.suggested_change: Keep the disclaimers in captions, where they serve readers who scan tables and figures, and delete three or four in-body duplicates — e.g. §5.4's 'Neither interpretation determines whether such variation is artistically appropriate' and §5.3's swap sentence tail — relying on §3.3 and §6.1 to carry the general limit once each.

findings.location: Appendix C.2 (pp. 16-17), sentence beginning 'The 24 permutations rearrange generated artist labels'
findings.issue: A label-permutation check is described and then disclaimed ('Their ranks are not exact permutation p-values'), but no rank or result is reported anywhere in the manuscript.
findings.reader_effect: The reader is told an analysis exists and how not to interpret it, without ever seeing its outcome — a dead end in an otherwise complete appendix.
findings.suggested_change: Either state the observed outcome in one clause (e.g. 'the observed labelling ranks first of 24 for k models') or delete the two sentences; the surrounding artist-coverage discussion stands without them.

findings.location: Table 2 (p. 7, 'ΔD versus FLUX', 'FLUX.2 Max 0 (baseline)') versus Eq. 7 in Appendix B.2 (p. 14, γ fixed at GPT Image 2)
findings.issue: The main results table takes FLUX as the comparison baseline while the estimating regression is parameterized with GPT Image 2 as the omitted category, with no note that the two choices are equivalent in the balanced panel.
findings.reader_effect: A reader who checks the appendix against Table 2 pauses to work out whether two different baselines imply two different analyses.
findings.suggested_change: Add a half-sentence after Eq. 7: 'The omitted category is arbitrary in this balanced panel; Table 2 reports the same differences relative to FLUX.'

findings.issue: Decimal style alternates between leading-zero-less prose values ('β = .999 [.893, 1.104]', 'error estimate, .801') and zero-padded table values (0.999, 0.801).
findings.reader_effect: Cross-checking prose against a table costs a moment of re-parsing on nearly every results paragraph.
findings.suggested_change: Pick one convention (the table style, 0.999) and apply it in prose, captions and appendices.

claim_fidelity_issues: §5.5 (p. 9): 'Source correction preserves FLUX's lowest point estimate while changing the evidence for particular model differences' is stated as a result, but only FLUX's corrected estimate (.872) is reported; no corrected estimates for the other five models appear in §5.5, Table 5 or Appendix C.5. The same applies to 'GPT Image 2 retains the lowest calibrated estimate (.579 after refitting)' in C.5. The wording is not overstated in substance, but it presents an unshown comparison as verified, which a careful reader cannot confirm from the manuscript.

§5.4 (p. 9): 'The fitted multipliers scale every contrast coordinate by about 0.45' generalizes a GPT Image 2-specific value (.438-.459) to the panel; Appendix C.2 shows FLUX's are .598-.694. This understates how unevenly calibration shrinks the models and therefore why the ordering changes.

Otherwise the manuscript is unusually scrupulous on claim fidelity: it states plainly that no model is established to beat the D = 1 no-distinction benchmark (§5.1, §7), marks the Monet-Sisley swap reduction as not independent evidence of perceptual confusion (§5.3), labels the GPT Image 1 interval moving above zero as a retrospective sensitivity rather than a confirmatory finding (§5.5), notes that calibration 'does not produce new images' (Table 4, abstract) and that 12-of-14 fold wins do not establish statistical superiority, and closes the abstract with 'These measurements do not establish perceptual fidelity.' No implication of unperformed perceptual or human validation was found.
summary: A disciplined, well-sequenced empirical report that a graduate reader outside the project can follow end to end. Its central distinction — detecting a name response versus reproducing labeled painter differences — is set up concretely in the introduction, operationalized with intuition before notation in §4.1 (a single-feature lightness example and three idealized generators anchoring D at 1, 0 and 1), and then carried consistently through results whose anchors are restated in every caption. The narrative has real turns (β ≈ 1 with D = 1.226; the lowest-error model showing the weakest Monet-Sisley alignment; calibration reordering the panel), Figure 1 and Figure 3 reward inspection, and the prespecified/retrospective boundary is never blurred. Four concrete weaknesses remain. The source-correction section asserts a robustness conclusion whose supporting numbers are reported for only one model, so its own heading's promise is unmet. One calibration sentence generalizes a single model's multiplier to the panel. Figure 2, the main results figure, wastes about half of each panel and pushes the substantive comparison into small insets. And the manuscript's admirable caution is applied at uniform intensity — about 29 terminal disclaimers in the main text — which flattens emphasis and slows momentum. All four are fixable within the 22-page and 155-word limits, mostly by adding one line of existing numbers, tightening axis limits and deleting duplicate caveats. Scores: expression 8.0, structure 8.0, new-reader understanding 8.25, engagement 8.0; overall 8.0625.
